newsitem.title: INDIA: India hurtles into political turmoil.
newsitem.headline: India hurtles into political turmoil.

text.p: India hurtled into political crisis on Sunday after the Congress party abruptly withdrew pivotal support for Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda's 10-month coalition government.
The shock move by the nation's oldest party cast doubts over talks between India and Pakistan and sent stock prices reeling.

Congress president Sitaram Kesri, citing what he called growing lawlessness and a drifting economy, told President Shankar Dayal Sharma that his party could no longer offer make-or-break backing for Deve Gowda's centre-left government.
Kesri staked a surprise claim to form a new government led by Congress, which finished a humiliating second in general elections last year behind the Hindu nationalist Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP).
The ruling United Front alliance, ranging from free traders to communists, said Deve Gowda would not resign but face parliament when it reconvenes on April 21.
"There is no question of the resignation of Mr Deve Gowda," United Front spokesman Jaipal Reddy said.
The shock decision by Congress to try to topple Deve Gowda's minority government came at an especially sensitive juncture.
The political tumult coincided with the third day of peace talks between Indian and Pakistani diplomats in New Delhi.
The negotiations began on Friday after a three-year impasse provoked by deep differences over the divided Himalayan region of Kashmir.
Rival Indian politicians agreed their domestic rumpus would have no impact on the dialogue with Pakistan.

But the political upheaval appeared to add another complication to the fragile dialogue between Indian and Pakistan, which have fought three wars since independence from Britain in 1947. Two of the conflicts were over Kashmir.
The high stakes in the talks were underscored by renewed violence in the Indian state of Jammu and Kashmir.

Police said a grenade attack wounded four civilians in the state's summer capital Srinagar on Sunday. Nine policemen were wounded at Kupwara police station near the Pakistani border when a device tied to the body of a slain Moslem militant exploded.
On Saturday, a car bomb blast in the state's winter capital Jammu killed 16 people and wounded about 70. Farooq Abdullah, the chief minister of Jammu and Kashmir, blamed Pakistan.
Congress's announcement, which capped months of strained relations with Deve Gowda, took financial markets by surprise and undercut stock prices in off-hour kerb trading.
"This is something totally unexpected," said Ravi Gopalakrishnan, head of sales at UBS Securities in the financial capital Bombay. "There's trouble ahead."
Analysts said the Congress decision was bound to affect investor-friendly budget proposals unveiled last month.

In the budget for the 1997/98 fiscal year starting on April 1, Finance Minister P. Chidambaram announced sweeping cuts in corporate and personal taxes. Parliament was scheduled to vote on the plan after it reconvenes on April 21.
Former finance minister and Congress leader Manmohan Singh said a change in government should not deter foreign investors.
"Why should it affect investor confidence. The economy has now acquired a momentum of its own," Singh told Reuters, saying there was broad consensus over economic liberalisation.

Congress, which has led India for all but four years since independence, said it might amend some of the budget proposals if it headed a new coalition. But it was not clear whether Congress, with 140 deputies in the 545-seat lower house, could muster enough support.
President Sharma could ask Deve Gowda to prove his majority in parliament or turn to Kesri. The Congress chief was expected to formally stake his claim before Sharma on Monday.
Waiting in the wings was the BJP, the largest single party which with supporters controls 194 votes.
The BJP said Deve Gowda's government was a disaster and Congress's proposed experiment would prove catastrophic. "One experiment collapsed, the other may not take off," it said.
